Industrial Chemistry · Unit 2 · Background reading · Draft

Part 3 Iron, Empire and the Nitrogen War: 1871–1918 From the proclamation at Versailles to the armistice: how a united Germany built the world's dominant chemical industry, annexed an iron field it could not yet use, and turned a fertiliser breakthrough into a wartime lifeline

Part 2 ended on 18 January 1871, with an Empire proclaimed and the dye works at Höchst, Bayer and BASF already open. This reading covers the forty-seven years in which those firms became the dominant chemical industry on Earth, in which an old, unfinished argument about German ironmaking finally gets its answer, and in which the same nitrogen chemistry that promised to feed the world instead kept an army supplied with explosives for four years of war.

Part 3 · draft 1871 – 11 November 1918 Höchst · Ludwigshafen · Oppau · Lorraine · Bad Homburg · Oberursel · the Taunus

By 1871 Germany was one country. It was not yet the world's leading chemical power — that took another thirty years — and it was not yet able to turn its own newly annexed iron ore into steel at all. This reading is about how both of those problems were solved, and about a third thing nobody in 1871 was trying to solve yet: how to make nitrogen fertiliser, and explosives, out of thin air.

Four threads run through it. First, the Gründerzeit boom that turned the four dye firms of Part 2 into industrial giants with laboratories of their own. Second, the iron and steel story Part 2 left hanging: Germany annexed one of Europe's largest iron-ore fields in 1871 and then, for seven years, could not use most of it. Third, dye chemistry's second act — a cartel, a fantastically expensive synthetic indigo, and two firms' first steps into medicine. And fourth, the hinge this whole reading turns on: a fertiliser process finished just before a war that needed it for something else entirely.

How to use the German sources

The same rules as Parts 1 and 2 apply. Words with a dotted underline are technical terms — hover or tap for the meaning, and check the glossary at the end. Source boxes give you the German first, then a Translate → button, then the author, the date, and links to where the text actually lives.

A note on this reading, before you start

This is a first draft, built from our own planning conversation rather than from a fresh full research pass the way Parts 1 and 2 were. The chemistry and steel sections rest on well-established history and should hold up; the Taunus mining stories have had more checking than most background reading ever gets, including a full read of the actual 1780 source Wikipedia cites — and that check turned up a real gap, described where it belongs, below. Treat this as a working draft to correct, not a finished reading.

Part one · 1871–early 1880s

The Gründerzeit: five billion francs, a crash, and the invention of the corporate laboratory

Germany's unification came with a cheque attached. Under the 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt, defeated France paid an indemnity of five billion francs — a colossal sum, intended partly to keep France weak and partly to cover Germany's own war costs. Much of it flowed into German banks, railways and industry over the next two years, fuelling a speculative boom so intense it gave its name to the whole era: the GründerzeitGründerzeit — “founders' era”: the boom years of company formation and speculative investment in Germany and Austria after 1871, fuelled partly by the French war indemnity., literally “founders' era.” New companies, new banks and new stock issues multiplied faster than the real economy could absorb them.

It could not last, and it did not. The Gründerkrach of 1873 — a stock-market crash that began in Vienna in May and spread through Germany within weeks — wiped out a great many of the speculative ventures the boom had thrown up, and tipped the German and Austrian economies into a prolonged downturn that historians once called, not entirely fairly, the “Long Depression.” The dye firms of Part 2 survived it: they were making a real, saleable product with genuine overseas demand, not paper promises. Bismarck's answer to the slump, in 1879, was to abandon Germany's free-trade policy and impose protective tariffs on both agricultural and industrial imports — a policy reversal significant enough that it is sometimes called the “marriage of iron and rye,” an alliance between industrialists wanting tariff protection and East Elbian landowners wanting the same for grain.

Hold on to this. A speculative crash followed by a swing toward protection is a pattern you will see again in this reading, and in the next one. Growth built on borrowed money, in any era, tends to end the same way — and the political response to the pain it causes tends to reach for the same tool: close the border a little, and hope domestic industry grows into the shelter.

The laboratory becomes part of the factory

The most consequential change of this decade was not political at all. Through the 1870s, Höchst, Bayer, BASF and Cassella each built something no chemical company anywhere had systematically built before: an in-house research laboratory, staffed with university-trained chemists whose entire job was to invent the firm's next product, rather than simply run the processes already known. This was a genuine German innovation, and one the rest of the industrial world — Britain and the United States especially — spent the next generation trying to copy. Part 2 already told you why Germany had the trained chemists to staff such laboratories: Liebig's Gießen students, and their own students in turn, had spent forty years spreading a research-based approach to chemistry through German universities that Britain's more practically minded chemical education never quite matched at the same scale.

The commercial logic was simple once one firm proved it: a single successful patented dye could earn back a laboratory's entire running costs many times over, and a firm without its own chemists inventing new dyes would eventually be left selling only what its rivals had already patented around. By the 1880s a large German dye works employed dozens of chemists purely in research — a ratio of scientists to workers unheard of in almost any other industry of the period.

A word invented to describe exactly this

The word scientist is younger than you might think. It did not exist before 1833, when the polymath William Whewell coined it at a meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science — reportedly needling Coleridge, who had just complained that "philosopher" was too dignified a word for men who spent their days with test tubes and frogs — and put it into print the following year, in an anonymous review of Mary Somerville's On the Connexion of the Physical Sciences. Before that, a person who studied nature in Britain was a “natural philosopher,” typically a gentleman of independent means — Humphry Davy, Michael Faraday — who did not need a salary to do it.

Coining the word in 1833 is not, on its own, evidence of anything happening in Germany: it is thirty years too early for that. But the word barely caught on for decades — British scientists mostly kept calling themselves “men of science” well into the 1870s — and it is exactly then, in the very decade this chapter describes, that “scientist” finally became ordinary, unselfconscious usage. That timing is not a coincidence, but the connection runs through Germany rather than out from the word: it was the German university research seminar — Justus von Liebig's teaching laboratory at Gießen from 1826, and the Wöhler and Bunsen generation who trained under his method afterwards — that first turned chemistry into a trainable, salaried career rather than a calling for the independently wealthy. That is the same pipeline of PhD-trained specialists that Höchst, Bayer and BASF hired straight into the new research laboratories described above. The word and the German factory laboratory are two symptoms of one underlying shift, the professionalisation of science into a paid, trainable occupation, rather than one causing the other.

The history of “scientist” How the word came to be (NPR) Coined in 1834, as a joke Coined to describe Mary Somerville?

Part two · 1871–1879

An iron field Germany could not yet use

Part 2 left a question hanging, almost by accident: why did Germany's first railway, in 1835, run behind a locomotive built in Newcastle, with British drivers, “nobody German having done this before”? The honest answer is iron. Germany's iron industry in the 1830s was small, scattered and mostly still charcoal-fired, decades behind Britain's coke-smelting and puddling capacity. By 1871 that gap had narrowed considerably — the Ruhr's coke-fired blast furnaces were growing fast, and small Taunus iron permits like those at Langenhain (1849) and Eschhofen (1867) show ironworking spreading even into the hills north of Frankfurt — but Germany was about to acquire, in a single stroke, far more iron ore than any of this could use.

The 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt that ended the Franco-Prussian War did not only bring five billion francs. It also transferred Alsace and most of Lorraine to the new German Empire as the imperial territory of Elsaß-Lothringen. Lorraine sat on one of the largest iron-ore fields in Europe, the minetteminette — the local name for the iron-ore deposits of Lorraine: abundant and easily mined, but heavily contaminated with phosphorus, which made them useless for the leading steelmaking process of the day. ore. On paper, Germany had just annexed a steel industry's future raw material in bulk. In practice, for the next seven years, most of it was nearly worthless.

The problem was chemistry, not geology

The leading steelmaking process of the day, Henry Bessemer's converter (patented 1856), blew air through molten pig iron to burn out carbon and turn it into steel. It worked brilliantly — but only with ore that was low in phosphorus. Lorraine's minette ore was the opposite: heavily phosphoric. Phosphorus in the finished steel makes it brittle, and worse, in a Bessemer converter lined with acidic silica brick, the phosphorus simply would not burn out at all — the acidic lining actively resisted the chemistry needed to remove it. Germany had the ore. It did not, yet, have a process that could use it.

A police-court clerk solves it

The fix came from Britain, not Germany, and from someone with no formal training in metallurgy at all. Sidney Gilchrist Thomas was a young police-court clerk in London who studied chemistry in the evenings and, working with his cousin Percy Gilchrist, a chemist at a Welsh ironworks, worked out the missing piece: line the converter with dolomitedolomite — a limestone-like mineral (calcium magnesium carbonate) used, once burned to a basic lime, as a converter lining that could react with and remove phosphorus, instead of resisting it the way an acidic silica lining did. or burnt limestone instead of silica. A basic lining does not resist the phosphorus — it reacts with it, drawing it out of the molten metal into a basic slag that can simply be poured off. The Gilchrist-Thomas processGilchrist-Thomas process (the “basic” Bessemer process) — patented 1878: a converter lined with basic dolomite or lime instead of acidic silica, allowing phosphoric ores like Lorraine's minette to be turned into good steel for the first time. was patented in 1878 and demonstrated successfully the same year.

Why this is the single most interesting node in the whole thread, for a hands-on parallel course. It stacks two separate pieces of chemistry on one historical hinge. There is redoxredox — a reaction involving both reduction and oxidation at once; here, the oxidation (burning-out) of carbon, silicon and phosphorus impurities from molten iron by blown air. chemistry in the basic converting reaction itself. And there is acid–base chemistry in the explanation for why the old lining failed and the new one worked — an acidic oxide (silica) cannot neutralise and remove an acidic impurity (phosphorus pentoxide) from the melt; a basic oxide (lime) can. It is a genuinely rare case in the history of this whole series where two different branches of the chemistry you teach separately turn out to be two halves of the same real industrial problem.

The effect on Lorraine's ore was immediate and total: overnight, minette went from a nuisance to one of the most valuable ore fields in Europe. German steel output, drawing on Lorraine ore processed largely in the Ruhr, overtook Britain's by the 1890s and kept growing through to 1914. Thomas himself did not live to see the scale of what he had triggered — he died in 1885, aged only thirty-five, from tuberculosis, having spent much of his final years travelling and researching rather than commercially exploiting his own patent as aggressively as he might have.

A corrective to “great men in laboratories”

Every other chemist named so far in this series — Liebig, Hofmann, Perkin, Kekulé, Graebe, Baeyer — trained at a university or a proper research institute. Thomas did his chemistry reading in the evenings, after his day job, and worked out the solution to one of the biggest industrial bottlenecks of the century as, essentially, a self-taught amateur with a cousin in the right job. It is worth remembering, next to all the professors, that this is also how some of the biggest discoveries of the age actually happened.

Meanwhile, in the Taunus hills · medieval–1919

Lead, silver, and a gold mine that never found any gold

Part 2 told you about the Taunus valleys as a place of cotton mills, paper mills and a wire-rope drive — light industry, powered by fast-falling streams. But the same hills have a much older, much stranger industrial history underneath them: mining, documented in this region since at least the late fifteenth century, and rumoured, on flimsier evidence, back to the Celts and the Romans before that. None of it is chemistry in the strict sense of this reading. But two of its stories — one a genuine boom-and-bust mine, one a fraud — are too good, and too local, to leave out.

Grube Silbersegen: lead, silver, copper and gold from one hillside

On the Gaulskopf near Cleeberg, on the eastern rim of the Taunus — further from Frankfurt and Oberursel than most of this series' local stories, worth being honest about that — sits Grube Silbersegen (“Silver Blessing Mine”), documented from 1459 and suspected, though not proven, to have Roman-era origins. It produced lead, silver, copper and even some gold, and had a genuine boom around 1700–1710, productive enough that contemporary accounts describe ore breaking “on all streets” around the works. Ownership of the mine was disputed so bitterly that a nineteen-year lawsuit at the ReichskammergerichtReichskammergericht — the Imperial Chamber Court, the Holy Roman Empire's supreme civil court, based for most of its existence at Wetzlar. ended only when the court commissioned an illustrated map of the site from the painter Hans Döring, to settle exactly what belonged to whom. Chronic groundwater flooding threatened to drown the workings for most of its life, and deforestation from smelting eventually grew so severe that ore had to be hauled fifty kilometres to a furnace that still had wood to burn. A final closure attempt came in 1919 — the same year, as it happens, that Part 3's own wartime section ends.

Why lead and silver keep turning up together

This is not a coincidence, and not really a mystery once you know the chemistry: silver substitutes directly into the crystal structure of galenagalena — lead sulphide (PbS), the principal ore of lead. Silver atoms readily substitute into its crystal structure in place of some lead atoms, which is why silver and lead ores occur together so often worldwide., lead sulphide, the chief ore of lead. “Argentiferous galena” — silver-bearing lead ore — is close to the normal case for lead deposits worldwide, not an exception. Wherever you find one metal in this family, it is worth checking for the other.

The Goldgrube: a hill renamed for a fraud

Near the Heidetränk-Oppidum — one of the largest Celtic hillforts in Europe, some 380 hectares, occupied from the 3rd to the mid-1st century BC, and close enough to Oberursel that genuine Celtic silver coinage has been recovered from it as recently as 2011 — stands a low hill that was, for most of its history, called the Hangelstein. Its modern name tells the whole story before you even hear it: the Goldgrube, the “gold pit.”

In 1719, two long-abandoned mining adits at the foot of the Hangelstein were rediscovered, and the hill was renamed on the strength of it. Mining rights were granted, on 16 July 1719, to a Freiherr von Creutz — in reality Johann Christian Würth von Mackau, an alchemist whom the German Wikipedia article on the site describes, without much hedging, as a fraud (Betrüger). Von Creutz was, at the same time, the “great and secret confidant” of the alchemy-obsessed Landgrave Ernst Ludwig of Hesse-Darmstadt, and the closest adviser to Landgrave Friedrich III of Hesse-Homburg. A shareholding mining company was formed that same year with the Landgrave and Landgravine of Homburg themselves among the investors — this was never a lone prospector's gamble, but a court-patronised venture with the ruling family's own money behind it.

The adits showed no workable ore from the very start. Von Creutz pushed ahead regardless, building an ore-crushing mill and hiring a smelter. By early 1722 the Landgrave's own doubts were strong enough that, rather than simply take his confidant's word for it, he brought in an independent expert: Johann Gottfried Schreiter. Schreiter's report, dated 14 February 1722, found no minable ore whatsoever, and costs wildly disproportionate to any conceivable yield. Work was ordered stopped. It was not, in fact, fully stopped: operations limped on intermittently for another seventeen years, extending the lower adit by a further twenty metres before final closure around 1739.

1722 is when the science said no. 1739 is when the money finally agreed. Seventeen years is a long time to keep half-heartedly digging a hole an expert has already told you is empty — and it is a very human, very repeatable story: a politically connected wish outlasting the evidence against it, not because anyone was fooled twice, but because closing the account was harder than leaving it quietly open.

Two later details push the site's real history much further back than von Creutz ever imagined. A Roman bronze coin of the Emperor Commodus (reigned AD 161–192) was found in the mine's spoil heap and reported by archaeologists in 1879, alongside identification of the approach track as Roman-built — suggesting the workings themselves may be well over a thousand years older than the eighteenth-century fraud that renamed them. And the mine sits strikingly close to the Heidetränk-Oppidum: its north-east rampart lies only about 150 metres away, with the oppidum's north-east gate facing the mine directly. Wikipedia's own article is careful to call any connection between the Celtic settlement and the mine “possible but not proven,” and this reading follows that same caution.

As historians, be on your guard! — what a 41-year-old eyewitness account does and doesn't confirm

Wikipedia's own footnote for the 1719 renaming points to a genuine 1780 pamphlet: Elias Neuhof, Fürstlich Hessen-Homburgischer Regierungs-Rath, Nachricht von den Alterthümern in der Gegend und dem Gebürge bey Homburg vor der Höhe — written by a Homburg government councillor just forty-one years after the mine's final closure, and digitised in full by the Bavarian State Library. We read all seventy-one real pages of the second, reworked 1780 edition (the digitisation runs to about a hundred page-images, but the book itself ends at page 71). It confirms the Goldgrube existed under that name and describes the general wall remains on the hill — but it does not contain the 1719 rediscovery narrative, von Creutz, or Schreiter's report anywhere in its own text; the closest it comes is a general, undated remark on its final page that past and recent ore-hunting on the mountain has always been “costly and unprofitable,” despite plenty of promising quartz. Neuhof's own foreword describes this pamphlet as a “second, completely reworked” edition of an earlier work of his — so either a first edition (not yet located) carries the fuller story Wikipedia's page number points to, or that footnote is attached to the wrong publication. Worth chasing before this box goes final.

Elias Neuhof, foreword to Nachricht von den Alterthümern… (Homburg vor der Höhe, 1780)

„In nachstehenden wenigen Bogen erscheinet dermahlen die zweyte, ganz umgearbeitete, vermehrt und verbesserte Auflage, meiner Nachrichten von unserer Gegend.“

Translate

“In the following few pages there now appears the second, completely reworked, expanded and improved edition of my accounts of our region.”

From Neuhof's own Vorbericht (foreword), dated Homburg vor der Höhe, 9 February 1780 — read from the Bavarian State Library digitisation while researching this reading.

digitale-sammlungen.de — full digitisation (German)

As historians, be on your guard! — a second person with almost the same name

While checking von Creutz's dates, we found that Wikipedia's own footnote for his death cites a Neue Deutsche Biographie entry for “Creuz, Friedrich Karl Kasimir Freiherr von” — a real, documented person, but a poet and philosopher who lived 1724–1770 and served a later Landgrave, not Johann Christian Würth von Mackau (the alchemist of this story, c. 1682–1732). Two men, a generation apart, with near-identical noble titles, appear to have been tangled together in a modern reference source. It is a small, live example of exactly the kind of mix-up this box exists to warn you about — caught, in this case, in the course of researching the very story you just read.

A third mine, closer to home, and a much slower ending

Near Glashütten, local history groups have surveyed over five hundred slag sites from medieval bloomery iron-smelting, concentrated in the 13th and early 14th centuries, with a 1319 arbitration decree explicitly naming iron smelting and charcoal-burning in the district. Several later medieval glass furnaces — the town's own name means “glass hut” — were built directly on top of these abandoned ironworking sites, reusing the same forest clearings and charcoal supply centuries after the iron trade there had died out. Glashütten's own glassmaking eventually faded too, priced out in the railway era by glass shipped in more cheaply from elsewhere in Germany — the same forces of integration and competition Part 2's Zollverein section described, working, in the end, against a small local industry rather than for one.

The irony runs deeper still: a railway line through Glashütten itself was once planned, and in August and September 1907 the route was actually staked out on the ground — surveyors' pegs in the soil, not just a line on a map — before the scheme was quietly dropped and nothing was ever built. Glashütten did not simply lose a fair fight to railway-connected competitors elsewhere; a line to its own door was surveyed and then abandoned, and no explanation for the decision seems to survive. The local Kulturkreis Glashütten history group, whose page on the village records the 1907 survey (illustrated with a contemporary 1908 map showing the planned route), does not say why the project was dropped either — which is itself a useful reminder that even a well-documented local fact can come with a gap no one has yet filled.

There is a second, later chapter of iron at Glashütten too, on a completely different site and a completely different clock from the medieval bloomeries above: the Historischer Steinbruch am Glaskopf, a quarry that mined BrauneisenerzBrauneisenerz (brown iron ore, chiefly limonite) — a common, iron-rich ore mineral, distinct from the sulphide ores (like galena) described elsewhere in this reading., “brown iron ore,” until it stopped being profitable toward the end of the nineteenth century — squarely inside this reading's own period, and centuries after the medieval iron trade above had already died out.

Naturpark Taunus / HessenForst — on-site interpretive sign, Historischer Steinbruch am Glaskopf

„Der Taunus ist aufgrund seiner vielfältigen Rohstoffvorkommen geprägt von der Geschichte des Bergbaus. Es gab viele Abbaugebiete, unter anderem am Glaskopf, wo Brauneisenerz gewonnen wurde. Als sich die Erzgewinnung gegen Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts nicht mehr lohnte, wurde dieser Steinbruch offengelassen und von den umliegenden Ortschaften zur Baustoffentnahme genutzt.“

Translate

“The Taunus is shaped by the history of mining, on account of its diverse raw-material deposits. There were many extraction sites, among them at the Glaskopf, where brown iron ore was won. When ore extraction stopped being worthwhile toward the end of the 19th century, this quarry was abandoned and used by the surrounding villages for taking building material.”

Text as displayed on the sign at the site, photographed on a visit to the Glaskopf, near Glashütten.

No online source — this is a physical sign, read on site rather than found online.

From quarry to owl sanctuary

The sign goes on to describe what happened next: once quarrying and building-stone extraction stopped, the site grew wild, and by the time HessenForst and the Forstamt Königstein turned their attention to it, forest had reclaimed most of the old workings, leaving only the steepest rock faces bare. Rather than leave it to keep overgrowing, the foresters deliberately cleared the quarry benches and exposed the rock again — because bare cliff is exactly what an UhuUhu — the eagle-owl, Europe's largest owl species, over 80 cm long. It builds no nest, laying eggs directly on ledges, in niches, or in crevices on high rock faces. (eagle-owl) needs to nest: no nest-building, just a sheltered ledge on a tall, undisturbed cliff. The cleared ground in front of the quarry is being left to grow into a wildflower meadow instead, feeding the insects that in turn feed other wildlife. It is a nice, very Taunus kind of ending for a nineteenth-century industrial site: worked out, abandoned, reclaimed by trees, then deliberately un-reclaimed by conservationists for the sake of one large, striking bird.

Taken together, these are not chemistry stories in the way the rest of this reading is. But they sit on the same hillsides as the cotton mills and paper mills of Part 2, they involve some of the same chemistry — ores, reduction, the metals this whole thread eventually leads to in Lorraine — and they are a reminder that not every industrial venture in this region succeeded. Silbersegen and the Goldgrube bookend each other nicely: one a real, working mine that boomed, flooded and finally closed after four and a half centuries; the other a fraud that never produced an ounce of gold, kept alive for seventeen years past the point an honest expert had already ended it.

Part three · 1878–1899

Dye chemistry's second act: a cartel, an eighteen-year gamble, and two new medicines

The 1881 Alizarine Convention

Once alizarin — Part 2's synthetic red, brought to market by BASF and Höchst within a day of each other in 1869 — was being produced by several rival firms at once, prices fell fast enough to threaten everyone's margins. In 1881 the main German alizarin producers formed the Alizarine ConventionAlizarine Convention — an 1881 price- and output-fixing agreement among Germany's leading alizarin producers, an early instance of the cartel behaviour that would eventually help produce IG Farben in 1925., an agreement fixing prices and dividing up output between them rather than competing it down further. It is worth noting for what it previews: this is the same consolidation instinct — rivals agreeing to cooperate rather than destroy each other's margins — that eventually produces the full merger of IG Farben in 1925, a story for a later part in this series.

Indigo: eighteen years and a fortune, to beat a plant

Natural indigoindigo — the blue dye long extracted from the leaves of the indigo plant, grown at industrial scale on plantations in British-controlled Bengal; chemically identified and eventually synthesised by Adolf von Baeyer and, at industrial scale, by BASF. was, by the 1870s, one of the most valuable agricultural exports of British India, grown on vast plantations in Bengal. The chemist Adolf von Baeyer worked out indigo's molecular structure through the 1870s and 1880s, and BASF bought the rights to develop a commercial synthesis from around 1880. What followed was one of the most expensive research gambles in the history of the chemical industry: roughly eighteen years and, by some estimates, close to twenty million Goldmark, sunk into getting a laboratory-scale synthesis to work at industrial scale and industrial cost, with no guarantee at any point along the way that it ever would.

It finally did, in 1897. Synthetic indigo, cheaper and more consistent than the plant-grown dye, devastated the Bengal indigo trade within a decade — a striking, uncomfortable example of a laboratory breakthrough in one country directly destroying an agricultural livelihood in another, a pattern worth sitting with rather than skating past.

From dyes to medicine

The same research culture that had spent eighteen years chasing a dye molecule was well placed to go looking for other useful molecules too. In 1897, a Bayer chemist named Felix Hoffmann produced a stable, chemically pure form of acetylsalicylic acid — marketed from 1899 as Aspirin, still in use today. The very same year, working on the same family of compounds, Hoffmann also produced diacetylmorphine, which Bayer marketed from 1898 as a cough suppressant under the brand name Heroin, believing at the time that it was non-addictive. Both drugs came out of the same laboratory culture, in the same year, from the same chemist — one becoming one of the most widely used medicines in history, the other becoming a controlled substance within a generation. It is a genuinely sobering pairing to end this section on, and this reading will simply state it rather than draw the moral for you.

As historians, be on your guard! — whose discovery was aspirin, really?

Sources are not in agreement, so these are our sources, and here is our best guess! The version above — Felix Hoffmann, alone, in 1897 — is the one that stood unchallenged for 37 years. But Hoffmann's supervisor at Bayer, Arthur Eichengrün, later said that he had directed the synthesis himself, instructing Hoffmann to make the compound without telling him why, and that he personally oversaw the first tests of it. No source credited Hoffmann as sole inventor until 1934 — a German encyclopaedia footnote, appearing the year after Jewish scientists began being forced out of German institutions, and at a moment when Eichengrün, who was Jewish, was in no position to object. Eichengrün survived deportation to Theresienstadt in 1944–45, and after the war set out his own account in full. In 1999 the pharmacologist and historian Walter Sneader re-examined the surviving evidence and concluded Eichengrün's version held up.

Bayer disputes this, and it is only fair to say why: the company points to Hoffmann's own laboratory notebook entry from 10 August 1897, and to the 1899 US patent, both naming Hoffmann alone. Neither of those actually rules out Eichengrün having directed the work — a junior chemist's notebook entry looks the same either way — but it means this is a genuine, ongoing dispute between a company's account of its own history and a historian's reappraisal of it, not a settled case of a wrong being quietly righted. What is not in dispute is Eichengrün's persecution, or the year — 1934 — in which sole credit first appeared in print.

Meanwhile, in the Taunus hills again · 1897–1910

Kaiser Wilhelm's Taunus: a rebuilt fort, a mountain railway, and an engine works

Part 2 already told you that Bad Homburg's own new electric tramway was extended in 1900 into a branch called the Saalburgbahn, built to carry spa guests up to the reconstructed Roman fort at the Saalburg — a project Kaiser Wilhelm II had personally championed since 1897. That one sentence undersells just how much of this corner of the Taunus, in the last years before this reading's war, was shaped by one man's personal enthusiasm for technology, archaeology and monument-building — all paid for, at least in part, out of his own pocket or the state's, at a spa town that had become one of his favourite retreats.

A cathedral for a spa town

Overlooking Schloss Bad Homburg, the Kaiser's own summer residence, stands the Erlöserkirche (Church of the Redeemer), built and personally funded by Wilhelm II and his wife Auguste Viktoria, who — per the church's own recorded history — “took a personal part in the preliminary planning.” Its cornerstone was laid in 1903, and it was dedicated on 17 May 1908 with the imperial couple present. The building deliberately echoes the great imperial cathedrals of the Holy Roman Empire, which is very likely why locals still know it by a grander nickname than its official one.

Erlöserkirche Bad Homburg — as recorded today

„Die Grundsteinlegung erfolgte 1903 und am 17. Mai 1908 konnte der Neubau im Beisein des Kaiserpaars feierlich eingeweiht werden.“

Translate

“The cornerstone was laid in 1903, and on 17 May 1908 the new building could be solemnly dedicated in the presence of the imperial couple.”

German Wikipedia's entry on the Erlöserkirche, drawing on the church's own published history.

de.wikipedia.org — Erlöserkirche (Bad Homburg), full article (German)

As historians, be on your guard! — a good story we couldn't source

Local memory holds that Wilhelm II, impatient to check on progress, would climb the scaffolding himself in his robes to inspect the building work. It fits everything else documented about his hands-on involvement in this project — but we could not find it in any written source while researching this reading, only as something passed down locally. Treat it as a story worth keeping, not yet a checked fact.

The Saalburg rebuilt, and a railway built to match — or rather, two of them

The Saalburg had stood as a Roman ruin on the Limes for over a thousand years before Louis Jacobi, a Bad Homburg archaeologist and architect, persuaded Wilhelm II in 1897 to fund and authorise its reconstruction on the strength of the extensive excavation finds already made there. Working under Jacobi's direction, it became what is still, by most accounts, the most completely rebuilt Roman fort anywhere on the old imperial frontier, with its cornerstone laid on 10 October 1900 and construction essentially finished by 1907. Wilhelm himself presided at the ceremony.

Confusingly for anyone researching it, two separate railway stations ended up sharing the name “Saalburg,” and this reading originally mixed them up. One is the still-running Bahnhof Saalburg (Taunus), a stop on the Taunusbahn — the steam and later diesel line running north out of Friedrichsdorf/Bad Homburg past the Lochmühle leisure park toward Usingen, Grävenwiesbach and on to the Gießen direction. Its building is an ordinary half-timbered “Landhausstil” structure, and it survives today as a restaurant, still served by regional trains.

The other — the one this section is actually about — is the terminus of the electric Saalburgbahn tram itself, opened 3 June 1900 and closed in 1935, standing right below the fort. It was designed by Louis Jacobi himself — the same man leading the Saalburg's reconstruction — in a “provinzialrömisch” (provincial Roman) style deliberately echoing the fort above it: a single-storey solid masonry building with a gabled roof, stone quoins and round-arched windows set against rougher masonry, with open timber-framed verandas on its gable ends. So the resemblance to Roman architecture is real, and by design, once you have the right building.

The beekeepers were real too

The old Saalburgbahn terminus building still stands, restored in 2005, and today serves as a Belegstelle — a queen-bee mating station — run by the Obertaunus beekeeping association. It is a genuinely lovely afterlife for a building Jacobi designed to greet spa-town day-trippers arriving to see a rebuilt Roman fort: over a century later, it is quietly doing agricultural work for the district's bee population instead.

As historians, be on your guard! — the same name, two different buildings

This reading's first draft described the wrong Saalburg station: it took “Bahnhof Saalburg” to mean the Taunusbahn stop (still running, half-timbered, now a restaurant), when the Roman-style architecture and the beekeepers actually belong to the Saalburgbahn tram terminus nearby — a different building, on a different, long-closed line, that merely shares the same place-name. It is the same kind of trap as the two men both called “von Creutz”/“Creuz” a few sections back: two things sharing a name are not automatically the same thing, and the fix here, as there, was going back to a named local source rather than trusting the first plausible match a search turns up.

An engine works on the valley floor

Down in Oberursel itself, on the same rail lines this reading has already followed, 1891 saw the engineer Willy Seck build a small engine he called the “Gnom.” The firm reorganised the following year as the Motorenfabrik Oberursel, and by 1900 had already built some two thousand engines. A building on the site still carries the name Motorfabrik across its front, a physical trace of this very period. The firm's real fame came a little later and a little further from this reading's chemistry: under French licence it built the rotary aero-engines that powered most early German fighters of the First World War, the Oberursel U.I and U.II among them, fitted to aircraft including the Fokker Dr.I.

The firm's later history runs straight through the rest of this reading's century. In the Second World War it turned to diesel research and became the principal manufacturer of the Raupenschlepper Ost, a tracked artillery tractor built some 12,500 times over for the German army. In 1990 it was sold into what was then BMW Rolls-Royce, and the same site in Oberursel builds Rolls-Royce jet-engine components today — meaning the “Motorfabrik” inscription on that valley-floor building has now outlasted three empires, two world wars and four changes of national government.

As historians, be on your guard! — a lead deliberately left out

While researching this section we found a documented forced-labour camp (Zwangsarbeiter-Lager) in Oberursel, 1943–45, written up in what appears to be the Verein für Geschichte und Heimatkunde Oberursel's own journal — quite possibly already sitting inside the same Mitteilungen archive being translated for a separate local-history project. We could not get past a blocked source to confirm the location, the employer, or the numbers involved, and this reading will not guess at any of that for you. It is left out of the account above entirely, on purpose, until it can be checked properly against the primary material rather than a search-engine summary.

Epilogue, decades later: the same railway becomes the U2 and U3

One more piece belongs on the end of this story, well outside this reading's 1871–1918 span, because it closes a loop this whole section has been building toward. In May 1910 the Frankfurter Lokalbahn AG (FLAG) ran new track out from Heddernheim to link Frankfurt's own tram network to both mountain lines described here: line 24 to Oberursel, joining the 1899 Gebirgsbahn up to the Hohemark, and line 25 to Bad Homburg, joining the Saalburgbahn's territory. For over sixty years these ran as interurban tram lines, through two world wars and the Frankfurt tram network's rebuilding after 1945.

Then, piece by piece, they were absorbed into Frankfurt's new U-Bahn. Line 25 converted to U-Bahn operation on 19 December 1971, becoming line A2 (today's U2) to Bad Homburg. Line 24 followed on 27 May 1978, becoming the U3 from the Hohemark, through Heddernheim, into the city. Both lines still run, essentially, along the routes this section has just described — which means a student catching the U3 at the Hohemark today is boarding a direct descendant of the steam-powered Gebirgsbahn that opened in 1899, on the same valley floor as the Motorenfabrik's rotary engines and, at the top of the line, within sight of a Roman fort a German Emperor personally had rebuilt.

Part four · 1898–1918

The hinge: bread from air, and then war from air

A crisis nobody could see coming from a laboratory bench

German agriculture, like every intensive farming system, depended on nitrogen fertiliser — and through the nineteenth century, the main industrial source of nitrogen compounds was Chilean saltpetreChilean saltpetre (sodium nitrate) — a naturally occurring mineral, mined almost exclusively in the Atacama Desert of Chile, that supplied most of the world's nitrogen fertiliser and explosives feedstock before Haber–Bosch., mined in one desert on the other side of the world and shipped in by sea. A chemist who could fix nitrogen directly from the air — which is, after all, roughly four-fifths nitrogen already — would free an entire industry from dependence on a single, distant, foreign supply.

Tried first, and left behind: the Birkeland–Eyde arc process

Haber and Bosch were not the first to fix nitrogen from the air at industrial scale — they were simply the ones who made it efficient. In 1903 the Norwegian scientist Kristian Birkeland and the industrialist Sam Eyde found that passing air through a powerful electric arc — deliberately imitating the way lightning fixes a little nitrogen naturally — forces some of the air's nitrogen and oxygen to combine directly into nitric oxide, the first step on the way to nitric acid and nitrates. The Birkeland–Eyde processBirkeland–Eyde process — an industrial nitrogen-fixation method (from 1903) that uses a high-power electric arc to combine atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen directly into nitric oxide, the first step toward nitric acid. Extremely energy-hungry, so only practical with very cheap electricity. became the foundation of Norsk Hydro, built around Norway's abundant, cheap hydroelectric power at Notodden and Rjukan — the arc consumes so much electricity per tonne of product that it only made economic sense where power itself was almost free. It genuinely worked, and genuinely fixed nitrogen from nothing but air and electricity. It just never came close to Haber–Bosch's efficiency, and once Haber–Bosch existed, the arc process was gradually left behind everywhere that lacked Norway's cheap hydropower.

Fritz Haber worked out a more efficient route at laboratory scale by 1909: nitrogen and hydrogen gas, combined directly under very high pressure and temperature over a catalyst, to make ammonia rather than nitric oxide. Carl Bosch, at BASF, then spent four years solving the ferociously difficult engineering problem of doing the same reaction at industrial scale — vessels that could hold gas at hundreds of atmospheres of pressure without failing was not something existing engineering had ever needed to do. The first industrial Haber–BoschHaber–Bosch process — the industrial synthesis of ammonia (NH3) directly from nitrogen and hydrogen gas under high pressure and temperature, first realised at scale at BASF's Oppau works in 1913. Before the First World War it was intended as a fertiliser breakthrough; during the war it became Germany's substitute for cut-off Chilean nitrate. plant opened at Oppau, near Ludwigshafen, in 1913. Before 1914, this was, commercially, an unproven fertiliser technology — expensive to build, not yet obviously cheaper than the Chilean alternative, its future still an open question.

Ammonia is not the same thing as explosives — the step this reading nearly skipped

Haber–Bosch makes ammonia. Gunpowder and high explosives need nitric acid and nitrates, not ammonia itself. The link between the two had already been solved, separately, by the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald in 1902: the Ostwald processOstwald process — a 1902 method for catalytically oxidising ammonia into nitric acid, using a platinum catalyst. It does not fix nitrogen from the air itself; it needs ammonia as its starting material, which is exactly why it paired so effectively with Haber–Bosch once that existed., which catalytically oxidises ammonia into nitric acid over a hot platinum catalyst. Before 1914 this was a comparatively minor process, since Chilean saltpetre already supplied nitric acid's raw material more cheaply than making ammonia specifically to oxidise it made sense. Once the blockade cut Chile off, the two German processes suddenly fitted together perfectly: Haber–Bosch supplied the ammonia, and Ostwald's process turned it into the nitric acid Germany's munitions industry actually needed. Neither process alone gets you from air to explosives — it took both, running one after the other.

Then, in August 1914, the question stopped being commercial. The Royal Navy's blockade of Germany cut off Chilean saltpetre almost immediately. Without it, Germany could not make gunpowder or high explosives at anything like the scale a modern war required — nitric acid is the essential feedstock for both fertiliser and explosives, and a country that cannot import its raw nitrate needs another way to make it, fast. Oppau was repurposed for munitions-grade nitric-acid production within months — ammonia out of Haber–Bosch, fed straight into an Ostwald plant built alongside it — and a vastly larger second Haber–Bosch plant was built from scratch at Leuna, coming on line in 1917. Without Haber and Bosch's peacetime fertiliser research, Germany's ability to keep fighting past 1915 or so is a genuinely open historical question — the “bread from air” process that was meant to feed the world instead kept an army supplied with explosives for the rest of the war.

Haber's other war

Fritz Haber did not stop at fixing nitrogen. He personally directed the German army's development and first battlefield use of chlorine gas as a weapon, at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915 — the first large-scale chemical-weapons attack in modern warfare. He held the rank of a German army captain for this work, and his wife, the chemist Clara Immerwahr, took her own life days after the Ypres attack, in a death some historians connect to her opposition to his work, though the sources here are genuinely disputed and this reading will not claim more certainty than exists. Haber went on to win the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — awarded, controversially even at the time, for the ammonia synthesis, not the gas warfare — a juxtaposition historians of science still argue over.

As historians, be on your guard!

Sources are not in agreement, so these are our sources, and here is our best guess.

  1. The exact scale of Haber–Bosch's contribution to keeping Germany in the war. Historians agree the process was essential to nitrate supply from 1915 onward; they disagree, and probably always will, on the counterfactual question of exactly how many additional months or years of war it enabled. Treat this reading's framing as the accepted shape of the argument, not a precise, agreed number.
  2. Clara Immerwahr's motives. Her death is well documented; the causal link to her husband's chemical-weapons work is argued by some historians and contested by others, who point to a more complicated personal and professional unhappiness. This reading states the connection some historians draw, without endorsing it as settled fact.
  3. The 1719/1739 Goldgrube dates. Covered fully in its own box above — flagged again here because it is the largest open verification question in this whole draft.

Before the next reading

Questions to think about

  1. Lorraine's iron ore was abundant from the moment Germany annexed it in 1871, but nearly worthless for seven years until the Gilchrist-Thomas process arrived in 1878. Explain, in your own words, why having a raw material is not the same thing as being able to use it — and name one other example from this reading, or from Parts 1–2, where the same gap appears.
  2. The Gilchrist-Thomas process works because a basic (dolomite) lining reacts with an acidic impurity (phosphorus) while an acidic (silica) lining does not. Explain this in acid–base terms, then explain the separate redox chemistry of the same converter blowing air through molten iron.
  3. BASF spent roughly eighteen years and a fortune developing synthetic indigo before it was profitable. What does this suggest about the difference between a laboratory discovery (Baeyer's structure, worked out in the 1880s) and an industrial process (BASF's 1897 synthesis)? Why might a company be willing to fund research for that long with no guaranteed return?
  4. Felix Hoffmann produced both aspirin and heroin in the same laboratory in the same year, 1897. Both were, at the time, considered promising new medicines. What does this pairing suggest about how much a chemist working in 1897 could actually know about a new compound's long-term effects, compared to what is expected of new medicines today?
  5. The Haber–Bosch process was developed to solve a fertiliser problem, not a wartime one, yet it is best remembered today for keeping Germany supplied with explosives after 1914. Using this example, discuss whether a scientist can meaningfully control what their discovery is eventually used for.
  6. The Goldgrube mine operated for seventeen years (1722–1739) after an independent expert had already reported no workable ore. Suggest two different reasons — one economic, one psychological or political — why a venture might continue long after the evidence against it is already in.
  7. The Oberursel–Hohemark and Bad Homburg–Saalburg tram lines of 1899–1900 are, via several conversions, the same infrastructure as today's U3 and U2. What does it tell you about how cities actually grow that a route chosen for one purpose (carrying spa guests to a rebuilt Roman fort) can still be doing useful work, for a completely different purpose, over 120 years later?

Reference

Glossary: the new words in this reading

These build on the glossaries in Parts 1 and 2 — look back if an earlier term (mordant, aniline, Zollverein, and so on) is unfamiliar.

WordWhat it meansWhere it appears here
Gründerzeit“Founders' era”: the speculative boom in company formation after 1871, fuelled partly by the French war indemnity.Ended in the 1873 crash.
minetteThe iron-ore deposits of Lorraine: abundant, but heavily phosphoric.Annexed 1871; unusable for good steel until 1878.
Gilchrist-Thomas processA “basic” steelmaking converter, lined with dolomite or lime instead of acidic silica, that removes phosphorus from molten iron.Patented 1878; made Lorraine's ore usable.
redoxA reaction involving both oxidation and reduction — here, impurities in molten iron being oxidised (burned out) by blown air.The core chemistry of both the Bessemer and Gilchrist-Thomas converters.
galenaLead sulphide, PbS, the chief ore of lead. Silver readily substitutes into its structure.Explains why Taunus lead and silver mines so often coincide.
Alizarine ConventionA 1881 price-fixing agreement among Germany's alizarin producers.An early preview of the cartel logic behind 1925's IG Farben.
indigoA blue dye, naturally extracted from plants grown on plantations in British Bengal; synthesised industrially by BASF in 1897.An eighteen-year, hugely expensive research project.
Chilean saltpetreSodium nitrate, mined almost exclusively in Chile; the main pre-1914 source of nitrogen for fertiliser and explosives.Cut off by the Royal Navy's 1914 blockade.
Brauneisenerz“Brown iron ore”: chiefly limonite, a common iron-rich ore mineral.Mined at the Glaskopf quarry near Glashütten until the late 19th century.
UhuThe eagle-owl, Europe's largest owl. Nests on bare ledges rather than building a nest.The reason the old Glaskopf quarry is now kept deliberately clear of trees.
Birkeland–Eyde processAn earlier (1903), far less efficient way of fixing nitrogen from air, using a high-power electric arc. Practical only with very cheap electricity.Foundation of Norsk Hydro; superseded by Haber–Bosch.
Haber–Bosch processThe industrial synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gas, under high pressure and temperature.Developed by 1909 (Haber) and 1913 (Bosch); repurposed for wartime nitrate from 1914.
Ostwald processCatalytic oxidation of ammonia into nitric acid over a platinum catalyst (1902). Needs ammonia as its starting material — does not fix nitrogen from air itself.Paired with Haber–Bosch from 1914 to turn ammonia into explosives-grade nitric acid.
Landhausstil“Garden-house style”: a picturesque, often half-timbered domestic architectural style used for some German railway buildings of this period.Bahnhof Saalburg (Taunus), the still-running station — not the tram terminus.
provinzialrömisch“Provincial Roman”: an architectural style deliberately echoing Roman frontier buildings.Louis Jacobi's design for the Saalburgbahn tram terminus, to match the fort above it.

What this draft still needs. The Goldgrube box's page-citation gap (flagged above) is worth chasing properly — either a first edition of Neuhof's pamphlet, or a different Neuhof work, before this box is called finished; now that we have Neuhof's own fold-out map in front of us, it's worth checking closely for the Goldgrube/Hangelstein place-name itself, in the period spelling. The Grube Silbersegen map by Hans Döring, and photographs of the old Saalburgbahn terminus building both in tram-era use and as today's bee mating station, would fit the same gallery convention already used for the Neuhof map and Part 2's Hardertsmühle. The Oberursel forced-labour camp lead is deliberately unwritten until it can be checked against the Verein für Geschichte und Heimatkunde Oberursel's own material rather than a search-engine summary. Iron/steel and dye-chemistry sections are built from well-established secondary history and are closer to ready, but have not had the same page-by-page primary-source check the Goldgrube box just had.
